working_title: Small changes that made work feel better

exercise.part_title: Small Changes that Made Work Feel Better
exercise.instructions: You are going to read four profiles of people who describe a workplace change that improved their daily experience. For questions 43–52, choose from the profiles A–D. The profiles may be chosen more than once.
exercise.matching_intro: All four people describe a change in work organisation that improved their own daily experience, but the valued benefit differs.

A.label: A
A.text: As a designer and analyst, my work requires deep concentration. However, constant small interruptions made it difficult to finish complex tasks. Our team introduced agreed no-meeting focus blocks, allowing me to plan my questions for later instead of messaging immediately. This change has been beneficial as I can now finish one demanding task without switching attention. However, these focus periods can make quick collaboration less convenient. While I would keep the focus blocks, I wouldn't use them for the whole day. I value concentration and clear boundaries, not isolation.

B.label: B
B.text: Fixed start times used to create avoidable daily stress for me, especially with my caring responsibilities. Now, I have the flexibility to choose when to start and end work within an agreed range. This requires clearer handovers with colleagues on different schedules, but I appreciate having control over my time more than working fewer hours. For me, predictability plus choice is more important than total freedom. I am practical and autonomy-focused, aware of the need for team coordination.

C.label: C
C.text: When I was asked to mentor a newcomer, I initially saw it as extra work. I accepted because the team needed help, but explaining familiar tasks took patience and exposed habits I never questioned. Over time, I learned to explain the reasons behind procedures, which improved my understanding of my role. I now find satisfaction in seeing the newcomer become independent. I value feeling useful to another person more than I expected. Initially reluctant, I am now quietly proud.

D.label: D
D.text: In my team, we often complained about recurring operational problems without solving them. We started having short scheduled problem-solving meetings where one person brings an issue, and we record one agreed next action. These sessions can become repetitive if there is no decision or follow-up, but I value shared responsibility when discussion leads to action. I am collaborative but impatient with empty meetings, and I appreciate when teamwork results in tangible solutions.

questions.prompt: Which person appreciates having control over their schedule?
questions.evidence: Now, I have the flexibility to choose when to start and end work within an agreed range.
questions.rationale: B describes having control over their work schedule, which they value more than working fewer hours.

questions.prompt: Who finds satisfaction in helping someone else become independent?
questions.evidence: I now find satisfaction in seeing the newcomer become independent.
questions.rationale: C finds satisfaction in mentoring a newcomer and helping them become independent.

questions.prompt: Which person values concentration and clear boundaries?
questions.evidence: I value concentration and clear boundaries, not isolation.
questions.rationale: A values concentration and clear boundaries due to the introduction of no-meeting focus blocks.

questions.prompt: Who mentions the need for clearer handovers with colleagues?
questions.evidence: This requires clearer handovers with colleagues on different schedules.
questions.rationale: B mentions that having flexible start and end times requires clearer handovers with colleagues.

questions.prompt: Which person initially saw a new responsibility as extra work?
questions.evidence: When I was asked to mentor a newcomer, I initially saw it as extra work.
questions.rationale: C initially viewed mentoring a newcomer as extra work.

questions.prompt: Who finds regular meetings can become repetitive?
questions.evidence: These sessions can become repetitive if there is no decision or follow-up.
questions.rationale: D finds problem-solving meetings can become repetitive without decisions or follow-up.

questions.prompt: Which person values shared responsibility in problem-solving?
questions.evidence: I value shared responsibility when discussion leads to action.
questions.rationale: D values shared responsibility in problem-solving meetings when they lead to action.

questions.prompt: Who appreciates predictability plus choice in their work schedule?
questions.evidence: For me, predictability plus choice is more important than total freedom.
questions.rationale: B appreciates having both predictability and choice in their work schedule.

questions.prompt: Which person learned to explain the reasons behind procedures?
questions.evidence: Over time, I learned to explain the reasons behind procedures.
questions.rationale: C learned to explain the reasons behind procedures while mentoring a newcomer.

questions.prompt: Who values finishing one demanding task without switching attention?
questions.evidence: I can now finish one demanding task without switching attention.
questions.rationale: A values the ability to concentrate on and finish one demanding task without interruptions.

validation_notes.brief_fidelity_notes: The exercise aligns with the Content Brief by presenting four distinct profiles with different workplace changes and experiences.
validation_notes.style_card_notes: The style card is followed by providing differentiated voices and experiences across the profiles.
validation_notes.british_english_notes: British English is used throughout the exercise, adhering to the CEFR B2 level.
validation_notes.factuality_notes: No unverified claims about productivity or wellbeing are made; the focus is on personal experiences.
validation_notes.answer_validity_notes: Each question has a single, defendable answer based on the profiles provided.
